description:
A tracking page starts a lookup only if the customer typed an ID. Here the ID is the text "0":

```python
tracking_id = "0"
if tracking_id:
    print("Tracking parcel")
else:
    print("No ID entered")
```

A teammate says the lookup will be skipped, because "0 means empty". What does the code print?
explanation: The value is the text `"0"`, which has one character, so it is not an empty string. A non-empty string is truthy, so the `if` runs and prints `Tracking parcel`. Only the number `0` is falsy, not the text `"0"` — so the teammate is wrong.
options: No ID entered — the text "0" counts as empty
Tracking parcel — "0" has one character, so it is not empty
An error — you cannot put a string after if
No ID entered — Python turns "0" into the number 0 first

description:
An online store gives free shipping once a cart goes past ₹999. So a cart of ₹999 must still pay for shipping, but a cart of ₹1000 gets it free. The cart below is exactly ₹999:

```python
cart_total = 999
if ________:
    print("Free shipping unlocked")
else:
    print("Pay for shipping")
```

Which condition gives the right result for this ₹999 cart?
explanation: A ₹999 cart must NOT get free shipping. `cart_total > 999` is `999 > 999` → False, so it correctly prints `Pay for shipping`, and a ₹1000 cart would pass. `>= 999` would wrongly free the ₹999 cart, `< 999` reverses the rule, and `== 999` matches only that one value.

description:
A grading chain should label 90 and above as "A", 75-89 as "B", and 60-74 as "C". A developer writes the checks from the lowest boundary upward, and a top scorer of 95 comes out labelled "C":

```python
marks = 95
if marks >= 60:
    print("C")
elif marks >= 75:
    print("B")
elif marks >= 90:
    print("A")
```

Why does 95 print "C"?
explanation: An elif chain is checked top to bottom, and the first true condition wins — every branch after it is skipped. For 95, `marks >= 60` is already true, so it prints "C" and never reaches the checks for "B" or "A". The fix is to order the conditions from the highest threshold down.
options: Because an elif chain prints every branch that is true
Because the else branch is missing
Because the first true condition wins

description:
A shop gives a discount on any bill of ₹2000 or more. But customers billed exactly ₹2000 keep complaining that they never get it:

```python
bill = 2000
if bill > 2000:
    print("Discount applied")
else:
    print("No discount")
```

What is the bug, and what shows for a ₹2000 bill?
explanation: "₹2000 or more" must include 2000, so the test needs `>=`. With `>`, a bill of exactly 2000 fails and the `else` runs, showing `No discount` — the exact complaint. Changing `>` to `>=` fixes it.
options: > should be !=; it shows No discount
> should be >=; it shows No discount
There is no bug; it shows Discount applied
> should be ==; it shows Discount applied

description:
A fitness band should give one badge per day. But users with high step counts say several badges pop up at once. Here is the badge code for a 12,000-step day:

```python
steps = 12000
if steps >= 5000:
    print("Bronze")
if steps >= 8000:
    print("Silver")
if steps >= 10000:
    print("Gold")
```

What does it print, and why do users see a pile-up?
explanation: These are three separate `if` statements, not one `elif` chain. At 12,000 steps every condition is True, so all three run and print `Bronze`, `Silver`, and `Gold` — the pile-up. Using `elif` for the last two would let only one badge show.

description:
An app must turn one typed word — "lights", "fan", "tv", or "ac" — into an action, and reply "Not recognised" for anything else. Every choice compares the same word against a fixed value.

Which structure fits this best?
explanation: Comparing one value to several fixed options, with a default for the rest, is exactly what `match-case` is for — `case _` handles anything unknown. Four equality-based `if` statements would repeat the same comparison and need extra logic for an unknown word; they would not all match the same word. One `if` with `or` cannot choose a different action per word, and deep nesting only adds clutter.
options: A match-case block with a case _ for anything else
Four separate if statements, one per word
One if that joins all four words with or
An if-else nested four levels deep

description:
An insurer approves a claim only if the policy is active AND the claim is "medical" or "accident". A coder thinks all four lines below mean the same thing. To settle it, they test an inactive policy with an "accident" claim — which must be rejected:

```python
active = False
claim_type = "accident"
if ________:
    print("Claim approved")
```

Which condition correctly rejects this claim?
explanation: `and` is checked before `or`. Line A reads as `(active and medical) or accident` → `(False and ...) or True` → True, so it wrongly approves. Line B puts brackets around the two claim types: `False and (False or True)` → `False and True` → False, so it rejects — correct. Line C's leading `or` drops the active rule, and line D needs both claim types at once, which is impossible.

description:
A garden system waters a bed only when the soil is dry AND the tank has water. Two coders write it differently. Notice the inner `if` has no `else`:

```python
# Version A
if soil_dry:
    if tank_has_water:
        print("Watering")

# Version B
if soil_dry and tank_has_water:
    print("Watering")
```

Do the two versions always behave the same?
explanation: A nested `if` with no inner `else` is the same as one `if` joined by `and`: both water only when soil is dry and the tank has water, and both do nothing otherwise. So they always match; Version B is just easier to read.
options: No — Version A also waters when the tank is empty
No — Version B skips the soil check
Yes — both water only when the soil is dry and the tank has water
No — Version A checks the tank even when the soil is wet

description:
A signup form intends to reject non-numeric ages before comparing them, but the checks are in an unsafe order:

```python
entry = input("Age: ")
if int(entry) < 18 or not entry.isdigit():
    print("Invalid age")
else:
    print("Accepted")
```

Which input exposes the ordering defect by crashing before the validation message can run?
explanation: With `"x"`, Python tries `int("x")` first and raises `ValueError`; it never reaches `.isdigit()`. Numeric text such as `"17"`, `"25"`, or `"0"` converts successfully. The safe order checks `not entry.isdigit()` before any conversion.

description:
A toll booth needs a one-line label: "Heavy" above 3000 kg, otherwise "Light". Three of the four lines below are broken — one uses statement syntax, one swaps the labels, one is missing a part:

```python
weight = 2500
category = ________
print(category)
```

Which line is the correct one?
explanation: A conditional expression is written `value_if_true if condition else value_if_false`, so `"Heavy" if weight > 3000 else "Light"` is right. Line A is `if`/`else` statement syntax, not an expression; line B swaps the two labels; line D is missing the `else` part.

description:
A ward monitor should alert when the temperature reaches 38.0°C, but its comparison excludes the exact boundary:

```python
temp = 38.0
if temp > 38.0:
    print("Alert")
else:
    print("Normal")
```

Which test reading exposes the boundary defect?
explanation: The incorrect `>` and the required `>=` differ only at exactly 38.0. At that reading, the current code prints `Normal`, while the rule requires `Alert`. Values above or below the boundary do not distinguish the two operators.

description:
A courier charges by weight: under 1 kg is "Light", 1 to 5 kg is "Standard", and over 5 kg is "Heavy":

```python
weight = 3.0
if weight < 1:
    print("Light")
elif ________:
    print("Standard")
else:
    print("Heavy")
```

Which is the shortest condition that correctly completes the chain?
explanation: Since `weight < 1` is already ruled out, the value is guaranteed to be 1 or more — no need to re-check the lower end. Only the top edge is left, and 5 is included, so `weight <= 5` is enough. `weight < 5` wrongly pushes 5 into "Heavy"; the others re-test a lower bound that is already certain.

description:
An age arrives directly from `input()`, so it is text when the comparison runs:

```python
age = input("Age: ")
if age >= 18:
    print("Eligible")
else:
    print("Not eligible")
```

Which is the smallest correct repair?
explanation: `input()` returns text, and text cannot be ordered against the integer 18. Converting at the point of input with `age = int(input("Age: "))` makes both sides numeric before the comparison. Comparing with the text `"18"` would use character ordering rather than numeric age ordering.

description:
A library should charge a late fee when a book is kept for more than 14 days. But a book returned after 20 days shows "Returned on time":

```python
days = 20
if days < 14:
    print("Late fee applies")
else:
    print("Returned on time")
```

What is wrong with the check?
explanation: The comparison points the wrong way. `days < 14` is True only for short loans, so a 20-day loan takes the `else` and is called on time. The fee is for *more than* 14 days, so the test should be `days > 14`.
options: It should be >= 14 to include the 14th day
The else branch should print the fee

description:
A weather station should flag any reading below -50 or above 150. But a reading of 200 was called "normal":

```python
reading = 200
if reading < -50 and reading > 150:
    print("Sensor fault")
else:
    print("Reading normal")
```

Why did it not flag 200?
explanation: One number can never be below -50 AND above 150 at the same time, so the `and` is always False and every reading is called normal. It should be `or`: flag when the reading is below -50 OR above 150.
options: The else needs its own condition

description:
A player shows 4K only for a premium user on a line faster than 25 Mbps. This user is premium, but the line is only 18 Mbps:

```python
premium = True
bandwidth = 18
quality = "4K" if premium and bandwidth > 25 else "HD"
print(quality)
```

What is quality set to?
explanation: The condition is `premium and bandwidth > 25`. `premium` is True but `bandwidth > 25` is `18 > 25` → False, so `True and False` → False. The expression takes the `else` value, `"HD"`. Both parts of the `and` must be True to get 4K.
options: An error — you cannot use and inside a ternary
4K — the second part of the and is ignored
HD — the line is not faster than 25, so the and is False

explanation: The doors are shut, so the outer `if` runs. Inside, `weight <= 800` is `850 <= 800` → False, so the inner `else` runs and shows `Overloaded`. The outer `else` ("Doors open") belongs to the door check and is skipped.

description:
A gym gate opens only for a member who is active and has not already entered — so one pass cannot be used twice. This member is active and has not entered yet:

```python
active = True
checked_in = False

if ________:
    print("Access granted")
else:
    print("Access denied")
```

Which condition opens the gate now but blocks a second entry?
explanation: Both parts must be true: the member is active, and they have not entered (`not checked_in`). Here `active and not checked_in` → `True and not False` → `True and True` → True, so the gate opens. If they had already entered, `not checked_in` would be False and the gate would stay shut.

description:
A coder rewrote a four-line decision as a single line, and a reviewer says the meaning flipped. The applicant's score is 720:

```python
# Version A
if score >= 700:
    decision = "Approved"
else:
    decision = "Rejected"

# Version B
decision = "Rejected" if score >= 700 else "Approved"
```

What does each version store for score = 720?
explanation: In Version A, `720 >= 700` is True, so `decision = "Approved"`. In Version B the labels are the wrong way round: when the condition is True it returns `"Rejected"`. So the two disagree — the reviewer is right. A correct one-liner would read `"Approved" if score >= 700 else "Rejected"`.
options: Version A stores "Approved", Version B stores "Rejected"
Version A stores "Rejected", Version B stores "Approved"

description:
A post office charges: up to 250 g → ₹20, 251 to 500 g → ₹40, over 500 g → ₹60. A 500 g parcel is being charged ₹60 instead of ₹40:

```python
grams = 500
if grams <= 250:
    cost = 20
elif grams < 500:
    cost = 40
else:
    cost = 60
print(cost)
```

Which single smallest change fixes the 500 g parcel?
explanation: The middle band uses `grams < 500`, so exactly 500 fails it and drops to the `else`, costing ₹60. The ₹40 band is meant to include 500, so changing `< 500` to `<= 500` is the smallest fix. Reordering or touching the 250 line does not help, and turning the `else` into `grams > 500` would leave 500 matching no branch at all.
options: Change the else to elif grams > 500

description: A dashboard has mutually exclusive rating bands and needs a clear fallback for any value not covered explicitly. Which structure communicates that design most directly?
explanation: An `if`-`elif`-`else` chain makes the mutual exclusivity explicit: the first matching band runs and the final `else` provides a fallback. Carefully written separate `if` statements could also be mutually exclusive, but the chain expresses the intended one-path design more clearly and is safer to maintain.

description:
A data plan charges: up to 2 GB is free, up to 10 GB is ₹100, over 10 GB is ₹300. A user on 1.5 GB — clearly free — was charged ₹100:

```python
gb = 1.5
if gb <= 10:
    charge = 100
elif gb <= 2:
    charge = 0
else:
    charge = 300
print(charge)
```

Why was the free user charged?
explanation: `gb <= 10` is True for anything up to 10 GB, including 1.5 GB, so the first branch runs and charges ₹100. The `elif gb <= 2` can never be reached for any value at or below 10. Range checks must go from smallest to largest: test `<= 2` first, then `<= 10`, then `else`.
options: The free and top tiers need a lower bound with and

description:
A lock should say "Invalid card" when a valid card is used with the wrong PIN. Instead it stays completely silent:

```python
card_valid = True
pin = "0000"

if card_valid:
    if pin == "1234":
        print("Unlocked")
else:
    print("Invalid card")
```

What does this print for a valid card and the wrong PIN?
explanation: The `else` lines up with the outer `if card_valid`, not the PIN check. The card is valid, so that `else` is skipped. Inside, `pin == "1234"` is False, so nothing runs there either — hence the silence. A wrong PIN needs its own `else` under the inner `if`.

description:
A kiosk matches typed language codes, which are all written in lowercase. A traveller types "EN":

```python
lang = "EN"
match lang:
    case "en":
        print("English selected")
    case "hi":
        print("Hindi selected")
    case "ta":
        print("Tamil selected")
    case _:
        print("Language not supported")
```

What prints, and why?
explanation: `match-case` compares for an exact match, and capital letters count. `"EN"` does not equal `"en"`, `"hi"`, or `"ta"`, so none of the named cases match and `case _` runs, printing `Language not supported`. Using `lang.lower()` first would fix it.
options: Language not supported — "EN" does not equal "en", so no case matches
Nothing — match errors when no case matches
English selected — the _ case jumps to the first case

description:
A form should block a blank subject. But a ticket goes through even when the subject is just two spaces:

```python
subject = "  "
if subject:
    print("Ticket created")
else:
    print("Subject required")
```

What happens, and why?
explanation: For a string, only the empty string `""` is falsy. `"  "` has two space characters, so it is not empty and counts as truthy — the ticket is created. To block spaces-only input, the developer should test `if subject.strip():`.
options: Subject required — a string of only spaces counts as empty
Ticket created — spaces still count as characters, so the string is not empty
An error — spaces cannot be tested in an if
Subject required — Python removes the spaces first

description:
A dispatcher checks a robot in order. Right now it has an order but no free slot yet:

```python
has_order = True
slot_free = False
zone = ""

if has_order and slot_free:
    print("Robot dispatched")
elif has_order and not slot_free:
    print("Order queued — waiting for a slot")
elif not has_order and zone:
    print("Idle move to zone")
else:
    print("Robot idle")
```

Which one line prints?
explanation: First test: `has_order and slot_free` → `True and False` → False. Next: `has_order and not slot_free` → `True and True` → True, so it prints `Order queued — waiting for a slot`. Once a branch runs, the rest are skipped; the empty `zone` is never even checked.

description:
A quiz records every result, but prints `Passed` only for scores of 50 or more:

```python
score = 45
if score >= 50:
    print("Passed")
print("Result recorded")
```

What does the program print?
explanation: `score >= 50` is False, so Python skips the indented `print("Passed")`. The final print is outside the `if` block, so it still runs. The program prints only `Result recorded`.

description:
A clinic calls a reading "Normal" only from 90 to 120, and both 90 and 120 themselves count as normal:

```python
systolic = 110
if ________:
    print("Normal")
else:
    print("Check with doctor")
```

Which condition keeps 90 and 120 as normal, without calling every value normal?
explanation: The band includes both ends, and Python lets you chain it as `90 <= systolic <= 120`. Line A uses strict `<`/`>` and wrongly drops 90 and 120; line B with `or` is true for every number; line C can only be true if one value equals both 90 and 120, which is impossible.

description:
A colleague says one line in this shipping code can never run, whatever the tier is:

```python
tier = "gold"
if tier == "gold":
    print("Free next-day delivery")
elif tier == "gold":
    print("Free standard delivery")
else:
    print("Paid delivery")
```

Which line can never run, and what does a "gold" customer see?
explanation: The `elif` repeats the exact test of the `if`. If the `if` is True, the `elif` is never reached; if the `if` is False, the same `elif` is also False. So the second line can never run. For `"gold"`, the `if` runs and shows `Free next-day delivery`.
options: The if and the elif both

description:
A quiz marks a score of exactly 60 as "Qualified" — 60 counts as a pass. Of the lines below, one fails a score of exactly 60, one is not valid syntax, and one swaps the labels:

```python
score = 60
status = ________
print(status)
```

Which line is correct?
explanation: Since 60 passes, the test needs `>=`, with the labels in the right order: `"Qualified" if score >= 60 else "Try again"`. Line A uses `>`, which fails a score of exactly 60; line C is statement syntax, not an expression; line D puts the labels the wrong way round.

description:
A store should alert to reorder when stock drops below 20, but stay quiet when stock is exactly 20. The stock below is exactly 20:

```python
stock = 20
if ________:
    print("Reorder now")
```

Which condition stays quiet at 20 but would alert at 19?
explanation: "Below 20" means strictly less than 20, so `stock < 20` is `20 < 20` → False and stays quiet, while 19 would alert. `stock <= 20` would wrongly alert at 20, `stock > 20` reverses the rule, and `stock == 20` matches only 20.

description:
A reviewer worries the two-`if` heater code might set the value twice, or disagree with the `if`/`else` version for some temperature:

```python
# Version A
if temp < 18:
    heater = "ON"
else:
    heater = "OFF"

# Version B
if temp < 18:
    heater = "ON"
if temp >= 18:
    heater = "OFF"
```

The two conditions are opposites. Can the versions ever give different results?
explanation: For any temperature, exactly one of `temp < 18` and `temp >= 18` is True — they are exact opposites that cover every case. So both versions set the same value every time. Version A is still safer, because an `else` cannot drift out of step during later edits.
options: No — one of the two opposite conditions is always true, so both set the same value
Yes — two ifs always set the value twice

explanation: No. For ₹5000, Version A's outer `if` is False, so nothing prints. Version B's combined test is also False, so its `else` runs and prints `Domestic large payment`. Version A's inner `else` only covers a large payment that is not foreign; Version B's `else` covers everything the combined test misses.
options: No — Version A flags small foreign payments
No — Version A prints nothing, but Version B prints Domestic large payment
No — Version B never checks foreign

description:
A parking gate reads the vehicle type "bike" and runs it through this match block:

```python
vehicle = "bike"
match vehicle:
    case "car":
        fee = 50
    case "bike":
        fee = 20
    case "truck":
        fee = 100
    case _:
        fee = 0
print(fee)
```

What is fee just before it prints?
explanation: `match` checks each case from top to bottom for an exact match and runs the first one that fits. `"bike"` matches the second case, so `fee = 20`. The `case _` default is only used when no named case matches.

description:
An ATM checks the typed amount before turning it into a number. The field holds "50x":

```python
entry = "50x"
if not entry.isdigit():
    print("Enter numbers only")
else:
    print("Processing", int(entry))
```

What does the code do?
explanation: `"50x".isdigit()` is False because the text is not all digits, so `not False` → True and the guard runs, printing `Enter numbers only`. The `int(entry)` on the `else` side never runs — which is exactly the crash the check prevents.
options: Crashes on int() with an error

description:
An uploader checks its rules in order for an 8 MB file named "report.pdf". The size limit is 5 MB:

```python
name = "report.pdf"
size = 8

if not name:
    print("File name required")
elif size > 5:
    print("File too large")
else:
    print("Upload accepted")
```

Which check stops the upload, and what prints?
explanation: The first check `not name` is False, because `"report.pdf"` is a non-empty (truthy) name. The `elif size > 5` is `8 > 5` → True, so it runs and prints `File too large`. The `else` runs only when both checks pass.

explanation: Neither named case matches `"9"`, and there is no `case _`, so the `match` block prints nothing. Execution then continues after the block and prints `Menu closed`.
options: An error because case _ is required

description:
A signup button lights only when both the name and email are filled. The name is "Ravi", but the email box was left empty:

```python
name = "Ravi"
email = ""
if name and email:
    print("Form ready")
else:
    print("Complete all fields")
```

What does the check decide?
explanation: `name` is a non-empty (truthy) string, but `email` is `""`, which is falsy. `and` needs both sides truthy, so `"Ravi" and ""` is False overall and the `else` runs, printing `Complete all fields`. One empty field is enough to fail the check.
options: Form ready — the name is filled, that is enough
An error — you cannot use and with strings
Form ready — a filled name makes the whole thing true
Complete all fields — the empty email is falsy, so the and is False
